title: The Copper Harbor
premise: Sable Montrose, a courier for the collapsing Republic of Vessany, carries the last diplomatic dispatches through a country dissolving into occupation. When an infant is abandoned at his safehouse with a note ordering him to forget its face, he recognizes the child as evidence of a massacre the victors intend to erase. Pursued by a former lover now serving the new regime, Sable must choose between destroying the records to save himself and smuggling them—and the child—to a neutral archive across the mountains. He delivers the truth at the cost of his own name, dying anonymous while the record survives under another's signature.
about_author: Yara Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging displaced-persons records in postwar Europe. She writes historical fiction about the people history forgets to name.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sealed Things
chapters.summary: Sable arrives in the river city of Copper Harbor posing as a bookbinder, his diplomatic codes hidden in book spines. Through his eyes we see a republic on its last legs: ration lines, whispered lists, officials burning papers. The emotional beat is wary routine—he has survived by being unremarkable, and he intends to stay that way.

chapters.title: Instructions in a Dead Language
chapters.summary: Sable receives his final assignment: carry the Republic's last true account of the Kellin Valley operation to neutral Velmark before the armistice signs it away. POV shifts briefly to his handler, Maren, who knows the mission is likely fatal and sends him anyway. The beat is quiet dread dressed as duty.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: During a curfew blackout, someone leaves an infant on Sable's step with a note: 'Forget the face.' He recognizes the swaddling cloth as Kellin Valley weave—evidence someone wants destroyed or preserved, he cannot tell which. His instinct to stay invisible wars with the small warm weight in his arms.

chapters.title: The Bookbinder's Hands
chapters.summary: Sable hides the child among his binding materials and works through the night, sewing documents into false covers. Flashbacks reveal he once lost a family to an earlier purge and chose forgetting as survival. The emotional beat: memory returning like a wound reopening.

chapters.title: Elsira
chapters.summary: Occupation officer Elsira Vant, Sable's former lover from university days, arrives to inventory 'cultural materials'—a polite word for confiscation. Their reunion is all courtesy over tea, each aware the other is lying. Told from her POV, revealing she suspects him but hasn't decided what that means yet.

chapters.title: What the Wet Nurse Knew
chapters.summary: Sable tracks down Odile, the midwife whose stitching matches the swaddling cloth. She tells him the child's mother was a clerk in the Kellin Valley garrison—the same garrison whose records Sable carries. Beat: the horror of realizing the baby is not separate from his mission but part of it.

chapters.title: Ledgers of the Vanished
chapters.summary: In the harbor customs house, Sable finds shipping manifests proving supplies meant for Kellin Valley civilians were diverted and sold. He copies them into cipher. Elsira nearly catches him; their charged exchange ends with her deliberately looking away—for now. The beat is complicity and its first taste of sweetness.

chapters.title: The Armistice Ball
chapters.summary: Sable infiltrates the victory celebration where the surrender terms are read aloud. He witnesses the victors' historians already drafting the official narrative, erasing Kellin Valley in real time. Elsira dances with him once and whispers: 'Whatever you're carrying, burn it.' Beat: love offered as warning.

chapters.title: Maren's Silence
chapters.summary: Sable learns his handler Maren was arrested three days ago and the network rolled up. Every contact he trusted is gone or turned. Alone with the child and the coded records, he understands the mission now belongs only to him. Beat: isolation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Informer's Price
chapters.summary: A desperate neighbor, Tam, offers to trade information about the bookbinder for bread rations. Sable pays him off but knows the betrayal is only postponed. From Tam's POV we see how hunger makes collaborators of ordinary people. Beat: the price of survival paid in small, shabby coins.

chapters.title: Night Crossing of the Weir
chapters.summary: Sable moves the child and half the records to a smuggler's boat on the harbor weir. The crossing goes wrong; a patrol boat sweeps the water, and Sable submerges with the baby wrapped in oilcloth, nearly drowning them both. Beat: terror transfigured—the moment staying invisible becomes impossible.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Tea
chapters.summary: Elsira summons Sable formally. She lays out what she knows: the boat, the midwife, the missing pages. Instead of arresting him, she asks one question—'Was it true, what they did in the valley?'—and lets him leave. Her POV reveals her own brother died there. Beat: two loyalties breaking at once.

chapters.title: The Archive at Saint-Aubin
chapters.summary: Sable reaches the neutral monastery-archive at Saint-Aubin, but the archivists refuse anything without provenance—victors' rules now govern even neutrality. He must find a witness who can authenticate the Kellin records. Beat: hope deferred; truth needs more than paper.

chapters.title: Odile's Testimony
chapters.summary: Sable returns for Odile, but she has been detained. He finds her in a holding barracks and persuades her to testify—not for justice, she says bitterly, but so the dead aren't reduced to rumor. Beat: grief converted into purpose, the theme of memory made flesh.

chapters.title: Tam's Choice
chapters.summary: Tam, wracked with guilt, warns Sable that Elsira's superiors have ordered the bookbinder taken alive. He begs forgiveness; Sable gives neither punishment nor absolution, only work: drive us north. Beat: mercy as strategy, and the fragile redemption of a small man.

chapters.title: The Road Through Ash Country
chapters.summary: The flight north through burned farmland, told partly through the child's growing presence—first words spoken in a hayloft. Sable realizes he has stopped being a courier and become a father of sorts. Beat: tenderness blooming inside danger, raising the stakes unbearably.

chapters.title: Checkpoint at Grey Ford
chapters.summary: A checkpoint traps them. Elsira is the inspecting officer. In front of her men she must choose: expose Sable or falsify her own report. She waves the cart through and resigns herself to treason. Beat: the climax of the love-against-duty thread—duty loses, loudly, quietly.

chapters.title: What Was Done in the Valley
chapters.summary: Sheltering in a chapel, Sable finally decodes the full Kellin record: orders signed, numbers counted, names listed—including the child's mother, who hid the baby and sent her out with the note. He weeps for the first time in the book. Beat: the full weight of memory, unbearable and necessary.

chapters.title: The Victor's Historian
chapters.summary: The regime's chief historian, Dr. Corvel, catches up at the border, offering Sable amnesty in exchange for the originals—history written by the winners, gently purchased. Sable refuses, understanding Corvel's offer is itself the confession. Beat: moral climax; the temptation to survive comfortably declined.

chapters.title: Crossing at the Salt Pass
chapters.summary: The escape through the snowbound pass with Corvel's soldiers behind them. Tam takes a bullet buying time; Elsira, now openly a fugitive, carries the child when Sable can no longer walk. Beat: sacrifice stacking on sacrifice, the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: At the Velmark archive, the records are authenticated and entered under seal—but Sable, feverish from a wound, insists they be filed under the names of the dead, not his own. Elsira signs as witness. Beat: triumph rendered as anonymity; the truth outlives the man.

chapters.title: The Face Worth Remembering
chapters.summary: Years later, Elsira raises the child in exile, telling her nothing of Sable except that he kept his hands busy and his name small. A young historian arrives asking about the anonymous donor of the Kellin papers. Elsira smiles: 'He asked to be forgotten. But you may remember the face.' Final beat: memory chosen over survival, love recorded after all.
